about: The shared authoring policy the /mentor command checks a lesson against (docs/mentor-authoring-policy.md). Its id goes into every evidence file (publish.py); a lesson checked against another version is not published. Change the rules by adding a version, never by editing this one in place. Content format: the lesson format Mentor imports (docs/mentor-command.md); this file adds no second schema.

rules.rule: Fetch, integration (merge or rebase), commit and publication (push) are four different steps, and GitHub is not the only real repository: every clone is one.
rules.bad: Q: What does git fetch do? A: It updates your code with the changes on GitHub.
rules.good: Q: You ran git fetch. Your files did not change. Which step is still missing before your branch has the new commits, and which command does it? A: Integration: git merge (or git rebase) of origin/main; fetch only updated the remote-tracking refs in your own repository.

rules.rule: Grade code in its own language. Rust is never checked by Python's parser; a predicted output keeps every sign, operator and the order of lines.
rules.bad: A Rust drill whose whole-body answer is parsed and scored as Python; or a predicted output accepted as '3 5' when the program prints '-3\n5'.
rules.good: A Rust prediction task with the exact expected output ('-3' then '5' on its own line), self-checked or compared exactly, never parsed as Python.

rules.rule: State every assumption that changes the solution: which attacks can interrupt, and when an action starts before an exact deadline is asked for.
rules.bad: Q: Can the player punish the heavy attack? (Nothing says whether a light attack interrupts it.)
rules.good: Q: A light attack cannot interrupt the heavy attack's last 12 frames; the player's action starts on the frame after the input. The heavy attack recovers in 18 frames. Can a 7-frame jab land before recovery ends? A: Yes: it lands on frame 8, inside the 18-frame recovery.

rules.rule: The front never prints the finding it asks the learner to recall, and an application problem keeps the numbers it needs on the card.
rules.bad: Q: The study found a 250 ms latency threshold for detecting delay. What threshold did the study find?
rules.good: Q: In the study's tapping task, participants first noticed delay at 250 ms. Your controller's chain measures 180 ms. Will these participants likely notice it in that task? A: Probably not in that task; 180 ms is under the 250 ms they detected, but the result holds for that task only.

rules.rule: A threshold from one study is not a universal limit, and a non-significant difference is not proof that two things are the same.
rules.bad: A: Haptic latency must stay under 250 ms for every controller. / A: The study showed vibration and sound give equal accuracy (p = 0.31).
rules.good: A: Under 250 ms for that apparatus and task; other tasks may differ. / A: The study did not detect a difference; that is not shown equivalence (no equivalence test was run).

rules.rule: Teach the words a question needs before asking for an explanation that uses them, inside the lesson's teaching, without a scheduled card for every noun.
rules.bad: Explain why the reducer must be pure. (Reducer and pure were never taught.) / Twelve term cards, one per noun in the snippet.
rules.good: A two-line teaching note defines reducer and pure in context, then one explanation item uses them; only the one term the outcome depends on becomes a card.

rules.rule: Capturing the same concept again revises its one lesson (a new revision with a reason) or adds a purposeful changed-context variant; never another lesson named by a timestamp.
rules.bad: lessons/20261118_0912-git-fetch.json next to lessons/20261117_2240-git-fetch.json, the same outcome twice.
rules.good: lessons/git-fetch-vs-merge.json, revision 2026-11-18b, correction.reason: 'item 2 was unclear (flagged); now names the remote'.

rules.rule: If every answer would be 'test with users' or 'check the source', the item must ask for a concrete prediction, classification, calculation or diagnosis instead.
rules.bad: Q: How would you know whether the new menu is easier? A: Test it with users.
rules.good: Q: Menu A needs 3 taps for Save, menu B 1 tap behind a long-press. Predict which one new users find faster and name the measure that would show it. A: Likely A, because a long-press is hidden (no signifier); measure time to first successful Save.
